title: Multitasking: Working slower with worse results
summary: Josh and Chuck explain why multitasking is largely a myth: the brain task-switches rapidly rather than truly doing things in parallel, incurring a switching cost that slows work and increases errors. They trace the term to a 1965 IBM computer ad, cover the psychological refractory period and processing bottleneck theories (including French fMRI work from 2010 and David Meyer's University of Michigan research), George Miller's seven-item working memory limit, ADHD and multitasking, productivity losses at work, dangers of distracted and eating-while-driving, media multitasking and academic performance, dubious studies on gender differences in multitasking, rare "super taskers" identified by University of Utah researchers, and tips like turning off notifications and using the Pomodoro technique. The episode closes with a listener email from Bob Giorsi, a former Spruce Elementary School student in the Pygmalion in the classroom experiment.
topics: Pygmalion in the classroom listener mail

segments.title: Opening banter and definition of multitasking
segments.summary: The hosts joke about the episode and introduce the idea that multitasking is really rapid task switching, which makes people worse at tasks. They note the term comes from a 1965 IBM computer ad.

segments.title: Origins of multitasking and computers vs. brains
segments.summary: Chuck explains that early single-CPU computers also task-switched rather than truly multitasking until multi-core processors arrived, and that humans face a processing bottleneck.

segments.title: Switching costs and the psychological refractory period
segments.summary: The hosts describe switching costs, the time lag when moving between tasks, and the psychological refractory period, in which response to a second task is delayed while the first is still processed.

segments.title: Brain hemispheres, French fMRI study, and response selection bottleneck
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a 2010 French fMRI study on prefrontal cortex splitting across hemispheres, the idea that two tasks are manageable but three are not, and David Meyer's University of Michigan work on response selection bottleneck and prioritization.

segments.title: George Miller's seven and working memory
segments.summary: The hosts cover George Miller's finding that average recall is about seven items, and how people chunk numbers like phone and Social Security numbers into smaller pieces to ease working memory. Multitasking relies heavily on working memory.

segments.title: ADHD and multitasking
segments.summary: Chuck explains that multitasking is hard for people with ADHD because it draws on memory, attention, self-regulation, and goal direction; people with ADHD have longer switching gaps and higher arousal and stress.

segments.title: Productivity and performance losses
segments.summary: Josh says studies show multitasking lowers work quality and increases errors, with up to a forty percent productivity loss from checking social media and email at work. Chuck gives a joking example of making a paper airplane and shaving a bunny.

segments.title: Distracted driving and eating behind the wheel
segments.summary: The hosts discuss smartphone distraction and crash data from a 2022 study, and NHTSA findings that eating or drinking while driving raises accident risk; coffee, soups, chili, fried chicken, and jelly donuts were named as risky foods.

segments.title: Multitasking and academic performance
segments.summary: A study found Facebook and texting linked to poorer grades while online searching and emailing were less related. The hosts note studies conflate distraction with multitasking.

segments.title: Notifications, focus, and reading habits
segments.summary: Josh recommends turning off phone notifications and describes struggles with admin days. Chuck describes superficial reading online, referencing Nicholas Carr's article, and both describe returning to reading novels and fiction.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Brief break before returning to the segment on the quality of multitasking research.

segments.title: Gender differences in multitasking studies
segments.summary: The hosts question studies claiming men or women are better at multitasking. They critique a study using a blank-paper key-finding task and a Penn Medicine connectome study that the media overextended to memory and social cognition claims.

segments.title: Media multitasking trends and super taskers
segments.summary: Media multitasking rose from about 16 percent of media time in the late nineties to 26 percent in 2005 and 30 percent by 2011. Chuck describes University of Utah researchers finding rare super taskers, about two and a half percent of 400 people, unaffected by switching.

segments.title: Pomodoro technique for focus
segments.summary: Josh describes the Pomodoro technique by Francesco Cirillo: 25-minute focused work blocks with five-minute breaks, and a longer break after four cycles, with notifications off.

segments.title: Listener mail from Bob Giorsi on Pygmalion experiment
segments.summary: A listener who attended Spruce Elementary School in the 1960s writes that he was part of the Pygmalion in the classroom experiment and that principal Leonore Jacobson is still living at 101.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck invites listener mail and the hosts sign off.
